narr: In this section, we'll explore vocabulary related to business trends and cause-and-effect relationships in English for Engineering.
We'll also look at how to structure short talks and recognize signposting language.
Let's start with vocabulary describing how business metrics change over time.
Rapid or rapidly means something happens very quickly, like a company expanding rapidly throughout Canada.
Sudden or suddenly means something happens without warning, like consumer interest suddenly decreasing.
Dramatic or dramatically indicates extreme or very big changes, such as dramatically improving customer satisfaction or dramatic growth after investing in new products.
Calm or calmly describes reactions that are steady and without much change, like markets reacting calmly to developments or consumers being calm over time.
Flat means there's no change at all, like profit being flat over two years.
Steady or steadily indicates consistent improvement or staying at the same level, like steady improvement over three months or sales improving steadily since March.
Now let's look at verbs that express cause and effect relationships, which are often described using conjunctions like 'because' or expressions like 'due to'.

rows.text: influence
Her grandmother influenced / had a considerable influence on Sarah's choice of career.
had an effect on
determine
Parental attitude largely determines how well a child adapts to school.
the main factor affecting it
motivate
A good teacher motivates their students.
makes them want to do something positive
facilitate
The flow of traffic through the town is facilitated by the one-way system.
made easier
provoke
His speech provoked an angry response.
caused, usually something negative

narr: First, we have 'influence' which means to have an effect on someone's choices or actions.
Next, 'determine' refers to something being the main factor affecting an outcome.
'Motivate' means to make someone want to do something positive.
'Facilitate' means to make something easier, like traffic flow being made easier by a one-way system.
'Provoke' typically means to cause something negative, like an angry response to a speech.

rows.text: trigger
The explosion was triggered by the heat.
started, usually something sudden and negative
account for
The tilting of the earth on its axis accounts for the change in the seasons.
explains
spring / stem from
Sid's determination springs / stems from his desire to improve the world.
is the result of
give rise to
The country's victory gave rise to a new mood in society.
contribute to
Mobile technology contributed to the information revolution.
was one factor influencing

narr: 'Trigger' means to start something, usually something sudden and negative, like an explosion being triggered by heat.
'Account for' means to explain something, like how the earth's tilt accounts for seasonal changes.
'Spring from' or 'stem from' indicates that something is the result of another factor, like Sid's determination stemming from his desire to improve the world.
'Give rise to' means to cause something to happen, like a victory giving rise to a new mood in society.
'Contribute to' means to be one factor influencing something, like mobile technology contributing to the information revolution.

rows.text: stimulate
Their child was given drugs to stimulate growth.
cause something to develop or function
generate
Her exhibition generated a lot of interest.
caused something to happen or exist
induce
The drugs may induce nausea.
cause, often used in a medical context
inhibit
A teacher's presence can often inhibit teenagers' discussions.
prevent them from being as free as they might otherwise have been
derive from
A number of benefits can be derived from this situation.
gained as a result of something

narr: 'Stimulate' means to cause something to develop or function, like drugs stimulating growth.
'Generate' means to cause something to happen or exist, like an exhibition generating interest.
'Induce' is often used in medical contexts to cause something, like drugs inducing nausea.
'Inhibit' means to prevent something from happening freely, like a teacher's presence inhibiting discussions.
'Derive from' means to gain something as a result of something else, like benefits derived from a situation.
Now let's look at nouns that express cause and effect relationships.

rows.text: chain reaction
The incident set off a chain reaction which affected us all.
set of related events in which each one causes the next one
effect, impact
The effect/impact of the film on the audience was very powerful.
note the preposition on
end, means
Does the end justify the means?
note how end here means aim or goal
origin, source
The accident was the origin/source of her later problems.
beginning or cause
precedent
There are several precedents for taking such a decision.
something that already happened and provides a reason for doing the same

narr: 'Chain reaction' refers to a set of related events where each one causes the next.
'Effect' or 'impact' describes the result of something, with the preposition 'on' often following, like the effect of a film on an audience.
'End' or 'means' refers to whether the aim justifies the methods used.
'Origin' or 'source' indicates the beginning or cause of something, like an accident being the origin of later problems.
'Precedent' refers to something that already happened and provides a reason for doing the same in the future.

rows.text: reason
What was the reason for his success / why he succeeded?
note how reason is often followed by for or why

narr: 'Reason' refers to the explanation for why something happened, often followed by 'for' or 'why'.
When listening to lectures, it's important to recognize how information is organized through signposting expressions.
A short talk typically has three parts: introduction, main points, and conclusion.

data.heading: Signposting Language
bullets: Giving an overview: As we'll see from today's lecture... / In today's lecture I'd like to look at... / In this lecture, I'll be focusing on...
Sequencing points: First, we'll look in more detail at... / Then, we'll move on to look at... / After that, we're going to see... / And then finally, I want to take...
Examples and explanations: So for example; An obvious example of this is; this can be understood as; In other words; How that works is; As I said; As we've already seen

narr: Signposting language helps listeners understand the structure of a talk.
When giving an overview, speakers might say 'As we'll see from today's lecture' or 'In this lecture, I'll be focusing on...'
For sequencing points, they might say 'First, we'll look in more detail at...' or 'Then, we'll move on to look at...'
For examples and explanations, phrases like 'So for example' or 'In other words' help clarify ideas.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Describe the Chart
data.problem: Look at the chart and complete the text with the missing words. (The chart shows the number of cars entering the downtown area of West City each day over an eight-year period, years 1–8; the totals rise for the first few years and then fall after year 6.)

steps.text: Identify the main trend: cars entering downtown increase for the first few years, then decrease after year 6.
Use appropriate vocabulary to describe the trend (rapid, sudden, dramatic, calm, flat, steady).
Complete the text with missing words that accurately describe the chart.

data.result: The completed text should accurately describe how the number of cars entering downtown West City changed over the eight-year period, using appropriate vocabulary for trends.

narr: For this activity, you'll need to describe a chart showing cars entering downtown West City over eight years.
First, identify the main trend: the number increases for the first few years, then decreases after year 6.
Next, choose appropriate vocabulary from what we've learned to describe this trend.
Finally, complete the text with the missing words that accurately reflect the chart's data.
